description: A comprehensive knowledge graph for GitHub Copilot best practices, covering core features, effective prompting strategies, code completion techniques, chat capabilities, security considerations, customization patterns, workspace context management, and AI pair programming workflows. facts.statement: GitHub Copilot is an AI-powered pair programming tool that provides real-time code suggestions, inline completions, and chat-based assistance. It uses large language models to analyze code context and generate contextually relevant suggestions as developers type. Copilot integrates directly into IDEs like VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains IDEs, and Neovim.

GitHub Copilot provides inline code suggestions as you type. These suggestions appear as ghost text that can be accepted with Tab, partially accepted with Ctrl+Right Arrow, or dismissed with Esc. Copilot analyzes the current file context, nearby files, and comments to generate relevant completions. Multiple suggestions can be cycled through using Alt+] and Alt+[.

Copilot's context window includes the current file content, nearby open files, file path, cursor position, and recent edits. It prioritizes local context (current function/class) over distant code. Comments immediately before the cursor position have strong influence on suggestions. The context window is limited, so proximity to the cursor matters significantly for suggestion quality.

GitHub Copilot Chat is the AI-powered conversational interface for Copilot. It enables natural language interactions for code explanations, debugging, test generation, refactoring suggestions, and problem-solving. Chat can reference specific code selections, files, symbols, and workspace context. Responses can include code blocks with copy/insert buttons and file references.

Copilot Chat supports slash commands for specific tasks: /explain (explain code), /fix (suggest bug fixes), /tests (generate tests), /doc (add documentation), /refactor (improve code structure), /new (scaffold new code), /help (show available commands). Slash commands provide focused, task-specific responses optimized for common development workflows.

Copilot Agents are autonomous AI assistants that can perform multi-step coding tasks independently. They can read files, execute code, use tools, interact with APIs, and make decisions to accomplish complex objectives. Agents use a permission system where users approve or deny tool usage. The Copilot SDK enables programmatic agent creation and integration.

Copilot analyzes workspace context including project structure, dependency files (package.json, pom.xml, requirements.txt), configuration files, and established code patterns. It detects language versions, framework versions, and library versions to generate version-compatible code. Workspace context ensures suggestions align with project conventions and technology stack.

Custom instructions are markdown files in the .github/copilot directory that guide Copilot's behavior for a repository. Key files include architecture.md (system design), tech-stack.md (versions and frameworks), coding-standards.md (style guidelines), folder-structure.md (organization), and exemplars.md (reference patterns). Custom instructions ensure team-wide consistency and project-specific best practices.

Effective Copilot prompts are specific, provide context, and state intent clearly. Use descriptive comments before code, specify types and interfaces, include example inputs/outputs, and break complex tasks into steps. Natural language prompts work best when they describe the 'what' and 'why', letting Copilot determine the 'how'. Avoid vague or ambiguous language.

Comment-driven development with Copilot involves writing detailed comments describing desired functionality before implementation. Write function signatures with parameter types, add inline comments explaining logic flow, use TODO comments for planned features, and describe edge cases. Comments immediately above the cursor position have the strongest influence on generated code.

Copilot can analyze code for security vulnerabilities including hardcoded secrets, SQL injection, XSS vulnerabilities, improper input validation, authentication/authorization issues, and insecure dependencies. Use prompts like 'analyze for security vulnerabilities' or 'does this follow secure coding best practices' to trigger security-focused analysis. Custom security review instructions can be defined in .github/copilot files.

Copilot code review focuses on security critical issues (secrets, injection vulnerabilities), performance red flags (N+1 queries, inefficient loops), code quality (function size, naming, error handling), and testing standards. Review feedback should be specific, actionable, and educational. Always prioritize security vulnerabilities and performance issues that impact users.

Copilot generates unit tests, integration tests, and test cases for edge conditions. Use /tests slash command or prompts like 'generate tests for this function' or 'write test cases covering edge cases'. Copilot detects existing test frameworks (Jest, JUnit, pytest) and generates tests matching project patterns. Specify test coverage requirements and edge cases in prompts for comprehensive test generation.

Copilot automatically detects language and framework versions from project files (package.json, .csproj, pom.xml, requirements.txt, go.mod). It scans for version constraints and generates code compatible with detected versions. Never suggests features unavailable in the detected version. Version detection prevents compatibility issues and ensures generated code integrates seamlessly with existing dependencies.

When custom instructions don't provide specific guidance, Copilot scans the codebase for established patterns in naming conventions, code organization, error handling, logging, documentation style, and testing. It follows the most consistent patterns found, prioritizing patterns in newer files or files with higher test coverage when conflicts exist. Never introduces patterns not found in the existing codebase.

Prompt files (.prompt.md) define reusable prompt templates with role definitions, instructions, and output formats. They support variables (${input:variable_name:description}) for dynamic prompts. Prompt files enable consistent, repeatable workflows for code review, refactoring, documentation generation, and analysis tasks. Store prompt files in .github/copilot or project-specific directories.

Migration instructions guide Copilot to apply transformation patterns during code modernization (framework upgrades, architecture refactoring, technology migration). Define before/after patterns, API correspondences, mandatory transformations, obsolete patterns to avoid, and validation requirements. Migration instructions enable automated code evolution aligned with migration objectives.

Copilot Chat supports context references using # (files), @ (symbols), and workspace scope. #file:path.js references specific files, @functionName references symbols, and @workspace searches the entire workspace. References ensure Chat responses are grounded in specific code context. Multiple references can be combined in a single prompt for comprehensive analysis.

Specify desired output formats in Chat prompts for structured responses. Request code blocks with specific languages, markdown tables, bullet lists, JSON objects, or step-by-step instructions. Use format instructions like 'respond with a JSON object', 'provide a markdown table', or 'explain step-by-step with code examples'. Clear format requirements improve response usability.

Use iterative refinement to improve Copilot suggestions. Start with broad prompts, then add constraints, specify edge cases, request alternative approaches, and provide feedback on partial solutions. Conversational refinement in Chat enables progressive improvement. Accept partially correct suggestions and modify rather than regenerating from scratch when appropriate.

Architecture.md in .github/copilot defines system architecture, design patterns, layer boundaries, dependency rules, and architectural constraints. Specify architectural style (microservices, monolith, hexagonal, clean architecture), module boundaries, data flow patterns, and integration points. Architectural guidance ensures Copilot suggestions maintain system coherence and design integrity.

Tech-stack.md documents exact versions of languages, frameworks, libraries, and tools used in the project. Include language version constraints, major framework versions, critical dependencies, build tools, and runtime environments. Detailed tech stack specifications ensure Copilot generates version-compatible code and avoids suggesting unavailable features or APIs.

Coding-standards.md defines style guidelines, naming conventions, code formatting rules, documentation requirements, and best practices. Include language-specific standards (PEP 8, Google Java Style), preferred patterns, code organization rules, and quality thresholds. Coding standards ensure consistent code style across team members and automated suggestions.

Exemplars.md provides reference code examples demonstrating preferred patterns, ideal implementations, and best-practice code. Include exemplary error handling, logging patterns, API designs, test structures, and documentation examples. Exemplars serve as concrete templates for Copilot to emulate when generating similar code in the project.

Security-focused prompts for Copilot include: 'analyze for security vulnerabilities', 'check for hardcoded secrets', 'verify input validation', 'review authentication logic', 'identify SQL injection risks', 'check for XSS vulnerabilities', and 'ensure proper error handling without information leakage'. Combine security analysis with specific contexts (payment processing, user authentication, data handling).

Performance-focused Copilot prompts identify N+1 query problems, inefficient algorithms, memory leaks, unnecessary computations, and scalability issues. Request analysis with prompts like 'identify performance bottlenecks', 'analyze algorithm complexity', 'check for memory leaks', or 'suggest optimization opportunities'. Performance review should consider both time and space complexity.

Copilot generates code documentation including function docstrings, API documentation, README files, and inline comments. Use /doc slash command or prompts like 'add documentation to this function', 'generate API docs', or 'create README for this module'. Specify documentation format (JSDoc, Javadoc, Sphinx, Markdown) and level of detail required.

Copilot assists with code refactoring to improve structure, readability, and maintainability. Use /refactor command or prompts like 'extract this into a separate function', 'simplify this logic', 'improve error handling', or 'apply design pattern X'. Refactoring suggestions maintain behavior while improving code quality. Always validate refactored code with existing tests.

Copilot helps debug code by analyzing error messages, suggesting fixes, explaining unexpected behavior, and proposing debugging strategies. Use /fix command or prompts like 'why is this failing', 'explain this error', 'suggest fixes for this bug', or 'help debug this issue'. Provide error messages, stack traces, and reproduction steps for effective debugging assistance.

Copilot explains code functionality, algorithms, design patterns, and complex logic using natural language. Use /explain command or prompts like 'explain how this works', 'what does this function do', 'describe this algorithm', or 'explain the design pattern used here'. Explanations help understand unfamiliar code, review pull requests, and onboard new team members.

Copilot scaffolds new code including classes, modules, APIs, and project structures. Use /new command or prompts like 'create a new REST API', 'scaffold a React component', 'generate a database schema', or 'create a test suite structure'. New code generation follows project conventions, detected frameworks, and established patterns in the codebase.

Copilot Agents can perform multi-file edits across the codebase for refactoring, migrations, and large-scale changes. Agents analyze dependencies, update multiple files consistently, and maintain cross-file coherence. Multi-file operations require user approval for each file modification. Use agents for tasks like 'rename this class across the project' or 'migrate all files to new API'.

Copilot integrates with GitHub workflows including pull request reviews, issue management, repository configuration, and CI/CD pipelines. Agents can fetch PR data, analyze code changes, generate review comments, create issues, and interact with GitHub APIs. GitHub integration enables automated code review, PR analysis, and repository management workflows.

Copilot Agents use a permission system where users approve or deny tool usage, file access, code execution, and external API calls. Permission handlers can be set to ApproveAll (automatic approval), PromptUser (interactive approval), or DenyAll (no permissions). Permission model ensures user control over agent actions and prevents unauthorized operations.

The Copilot SDK (available for Go, Java, JavaScript/TypeScript, Python) enables programmatic agent creation and integration. SDK provides APIs for creating sessions, sending prompts, handling events, executing tools, and managing permissions. SDK integration allows custom Copilot-powered applications, CI/CD automation, and embedded AI assistance in development tools.

GitHub Copilot CLI brings AI assistance to the command line for shell commands, git operations, and system tasks. Use gh copilot suggest for command suggestions, gh copilot explain for command explanations, and natural language queries like 'how do I find large files' or 'git undo last commit'. CLI integration streamlines terminal workflows with AI guidance.

Copilot prioritizes context sources in order: custom instructions (.github/copilot), nearby open files, current file content, established codebase patterns, and general programming knowledge. Explicitly referenced files (#file) have higher priority than workspace context. Understanding prioritization helps craft effective prompts and structure workspaces for optimal suggestions.

Strategies for accepting Copilot suggestions: full acceptance (Tab) for complete suggestions, partial acceptance (Ctrl/Cmd+Right Arrow) for word-by-word review, rejection (Esc) when inappropriate, and modification of accepted code to fit specific needs. Review suggestions critically, especially for security-sensitive code, complex algorithms, and business logic.

Copilot limitations include: may suggest outdated APIs, cannot access external services or real-time data, limited understanding of very large codebases, potential for hallucinated code, no guarantee of correctness, and possible security/privacy implications. Always review generated code, validate with tests, verify security implications, and ensure alignment with requirements. Copilot augments but does not replace developer judgment.
